newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen braced for Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen braced for Fed rate hike.

text.p: The pullback in U.S. stocks from their record highs in recent sessions has built in a reaction to a long-dreaded hike in short-term interest rates, which much of Wall Street now sees as an inevitability.
Market watchers said that stocks could absorb a 25-basis-point hike in short-term rates without a major reaction, although a larger hike would likely shock investors.
"If they raise rates 25 basis points, it's pretty much there," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney.
The Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets Tuesday to debate whether to raise short-term rates in order to cool the economy.

In a Reuter poll, 34 of 48 -- or about 71 percent -- of economists at banks, securities firms, consultancies and academic institutions said they expect the Fed to raise the federal funds rate at least a quarter point to 5.50 percent.
The Dow industrials were off about 50 points at 6828 in afternoon trading on Thursday, bringing the blue chip index down about 3.5 percent from its record closing high of 7085 set March 11.
Further damage has been done to stocks in high technology companies, hit in past sessions by growth-rate concerns, and in smaller company stocks.
Reflecting this, the Nasdaq composite index, while rebounding up about 11 points to 1260 on Thursday, is off nine percent from its January 22 closing high at 1388.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday helped further convince Wall Street that a rate hike was likely by stressing in testimony before the Joint Economic Committee of Congress the importance of prompt action to keep inflation at bay.
"It would come as a great shock if they don't raise short-term rates next Tuesday," said Alfred Kugel, Stein Roe senior investment strategist.
While the broad stock market appears to be bracing itself for a rate hike, market players are looking for groups of stocks that may benefit, or be hurt, by rising interest rates.

Traditional laggards at times of rising interest rates are the so-called cyclical stocks, such as paper, chemical and machinery makers, because their earnings are sensitive to the swings in the economy.

But analysts said the cyclical stocks have been underperforming in past weeks and could even begin to rally. Fed action to raise rates would be a sign of a strong economy, which could mean cyclical companies are due to post strong earnings in coming quarters, they said.

Interest-rate sensitive financial stocks are also typically hurt by rising rates. But that group has also been hit by profit taking ahead of a rate hike and might not be as vulnerable to a relatively small hike in rates, analysts said.
"If indeed the increase in the Fed funds rate is modest...I think (financial stocks) would rally pretty well in this market," Kugel said.

Investors often flock to consumer non-durable stocks when interest rates rise, but smoking-litigation worries could keep investors away from group leaders including Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, analysts said.

Stumbling high technology and secondary stocks, however, would also likely loose further momentum. "If they raise rates, that continues to pressure the secondary stocks, the growth stocks in general," said Robert Robbins, market strategist at Robinson-Humphrey Co.

Robbins said the stocks in energy companies, such as international oil and oil services firms, could benefit from rising demand in an economy that is heating up. These stocks are also in good technical shape, he said.

But if the Fed does not raise rates or hikes them only a quarter point, stocks may be kept in check by speculation over more interest rate hikes to come, analysts said. "Speculation about rate hikes probably don't end with what they do next week," Acuff said.
